newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asian Grain - S.Korea picking up more feed wheat.
newsitem.headline: E.Asian Grain - S.Korea picking up more feed wheat.

text.p: South Korean feed processors said on Monday they will probably buy more than 100,000 tonnes of feedwheat from Canada to cover their needs in February and March, effectively lowering U.S. corn imports in the process.
"Our clients are still looking for Canadian feedwheat," said a trader with a Seoul-based foreign grain trading house.

"Current feedwheat prices are offered at US$4 to $5 a tonne lower than corn prices which are quoted at around $145 a tonne (C&F) for January shipment. Local buyers are likely to buy the feedwheat below $135 a tonne for February shipment," he said.
The shift to feedwheat was a feature in trading in the corn futures market at the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) on Friday.

Corn contract prices in the CBOT were unchanged to lower on scepticism that U.S. corn export sales will remain active. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) cut projected exports to South Korea in 1996/97 by two million tonnes because Seoul is expected to switch some purchases to lower-priced feedwheat.
The December CBOT corn futures contract finished unchanged on Friday at $2.72-1/2 a bushel.
A trader said the Korea Feed Association was thought to be seeking at least 50,000 tonnes of feedwheat this week. He said the wheat should arrive before January 30 in Inchon and Ulsan.
Traders said the National Livestock Cooperatives Federation (NLCF) was also believed to be still looking for 52,500 tonnes of feedwheat or corn for delivery in February.

A trader with a Seoul-based U.S. trading house said freight premiums to South Korean ports from the Pacific Northwest and U.S. Gulf remained unchanged at between $13 to $14 a tonne and $24 a tonne respectively.

Taiwan may also tender for up to 54,000 tonnes of U.S. corn and 72,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat this week although buying could remain slow due to rising freight rates and the belief that U.S. corn and soybean futures will slide further, traders said.
"Most of the buyers think corn and soybeans could drop further, so they are likely to stay sidelined until futures prices drop, or if the market shows bullish signals," one said.

Grain importers in the Philippines and Japan, on the other hand, should remain quiet this week after covering most of their requirements or finding current prices too high for comfort, traders in both countries said.

"We've finished buying U.S. corn for January-March shipment," a major trade house official in Japan said. "There's no urgent need to buy for April-June shipment yet. We'd like to keep a wait-and-see stance for a while."
Japanese premiums for U.S. corn were unchanged at 97 to 98 U.S. cents a bushel over the CBOT's March 1997 contract.
China is approaching some Japanese trade houses to sell Chinese corn, but their offer prices remain too expensive to compete against the new U.S. crop, traders said.
Traders said they were also closely watching weather conditions in South American corn areas which may lure them back into the market sometime in the future, another trader said.
Japanese importers are now buying U.S. soybeans for early February shipment.
Philippine flour companies have stayed on the sidelines on to the belief that U.S. wheat prices remain overpriced.
"Prices should come down some more in the U.S. markets to reflect the bumper harvests in other wheat producing regions in Europe, Australia, Argentina and Canada," a Manila trader said.
